lessons.sub: Where, order, paginate — and the index error that teaches you the rules
lessons.goal: By the end you can write compound Firestore queries, read the missing-index error, create the composite index it asks for, and paginate a list with cursors instead of loading everything.
lessons.body:
1. Queries are built from filters, order and limits

A Firestore query starts from a collection and chains conditions: where filters documents, orderBy sorts them, limit caps how many come back. Every clause you add narrows the result, and every document returned costs one read — so a query that fetches 200 documents to show 10 is a billing bug, not just a slow page. Skillzify's community page, for example, asks for questions ordered by creation time, limited to the first page, instead of pulling the whole collection and sorting in JavaScript.

2. The composite index rule

Firestore can answer a query only if an index exists for that exact combination of fields. Single-field indexes are automatic; the moment you combine a range filter on one field with an order on another, or filter on two fields, Firestore refuses and returns an error containing a direct link to create the missing composite index. That error is not a failure — it is the database telling you exactly what it needs. Create the index in the console, wait for it to build, and the same query works.

3. What queries cannot do

Firestore has no joins, no full-text search and no server-side aggregation. You cannot ask for documents where any of five fields matches a substring, and you cannot ask the server to count or sum. Those jobs belong to a different layer: denormalised fields you maintain on write, a search service, or a small aggregation document updated by a Cloud Function. Designing around these limits is the real skill — the query syntax itself takes an afternoon.

import { collection, query, where, orderBy, limit, startAfter, getDocs } from "firebase/firestore";

const q = query(
  collection(db, "questions"),
  where("section", "==", "beginner"),
  where("answered", "==", true),
  orderBy("createdAt", "desc"),
  limit(10)
);
// First page: getDocs(q). Next page: same query plus startAfter(lastDoc).

Pagination uses a cursor: the last document of the page you just showed. Pass it to startAfter and Firestore returns the next slice. Never use offset for paging through large lists — it still reads and charges for every skipped document.
lessons.task: In the Skillzify community, write a query that fetches the 10 most recent answered questions for one section. Then add a second where clause, trigger the missing-index error on purpose, follow its link to create the composite index, and re-run the query. Finally, implement a Load more button using startAfter with the last visible document as the cursor.
checks: Why does Firestore refuse a query that combines a filter on one field with an order on another?
No index exists for that field combination. Single-field indexes are automatic, but compound combinations need a composite index, which the error message links you to create.
Why is startAfter better than offset for pagination?
startAfter resumes from a cursor document, while offset still reads and bills for every document it skips.
interview: A query needs a composite index — what does that tell you about how Firestore executes queries?
Firestore answers queries from pre-built indexes, not by scanning documents. A query without a matching index cannot run, which is why reads stay fast and predictable at scale.
How would you implement search across lesson titles in Firestore?
Firestore has no full-text search. Maintain a lowercase keyword array on write and query it with array-contains, or use a dedicated search service for real text search.

lessons.sub: Your app keeps working when the network does not
lessons.goal: By the end you can enable Firestore offline persistence, explain what happens to reads and writes while offline, and describe how pending writes sync and can conflict when the connection returns.
lessons.body:
1. Turning the cache on

Firestore can keep a local copy of the data your app has already read, so the app keeps working with no network at all. On the web you enable it with persistent local cache backed by IndexedDB; on Android it is on by default. Once enabled, reads are served from the cache when the server is unreachable, and the app behaves as if the data is simply there. This is why a learner on a train can still open Skillzify lessons and see their progress — the data was cached on earlier visits.

2. Writes queue, they do not fail

When offline, a write does not throw an error. Firestore stores it in a local queue and applies it to the cached data immediately, so the UI updates as if the write succeeded. When the connection returns, the queued writes are sent to the server in order. Your code should treat a write as done locally and listen for the server confirmation separately, rather than assuming the network is always there.

3. Knowing what is cached and what is confirmed

Every snapshot carries metadata: whether it came from the cache and whether it has pending writes. Showing a small offline or syncing indicator from that metadata is the difference between an app that feels broken and one that feels honest. The hard edge is conflict: if two devices changed the same field while offline, the last write to reach the server wins at the field level, which is exactly why Skillzify merges per field with rules like union for lessons and max for XP instead of trusting last-write-wins for everything.

import { initializeFirestore, persistentLocalCache, persistentMultipleTabManager } from "firebase/firestore";

const db = initializeFirestore(app, {
  localCache: persistentLocalCache({
    tabManager: persistentMultipleTabManager()
  })
});

// In a snapshot listener, check the truth of what you see:
onSnapshot(docRef, (snap) => {
  const fromCache = snap.metadata.fromCache;
  const pending = snap.metadata.hasPendingWrites;
  render(snap.data(), { fromCache, pending });
});

The multiple-tab manager matters: without it, two tabs of the same site can fight over the IndexedDB cache. With it, tabs share one cache cleanly.
lessons.task: Enable persistent local cache in a copy of the Skillzify web app. Load your profile page, go offline in DevTools, reload, and confirm your data still renders with a fromCache indicator. Then complete a lesson while offline, go back online, and watch hasPendingWrites clear as the write syncs.
checks: What happens to a Firestore write made while the device is offline?
It is queued locally, applied to the cache immediately so the UI updates, and sent to the server in order when the connection returns.
How can your UI tell cached data apart from server-confirmed data?
Snapshot metadata: fromCache says the data came from the local cache, and hasPendingWrites says local writes have not reached the server yet.
interview: Why is offline support a data-design decision, not just a toggle?
Because conflicts are resolved by your merge rules. Last-write-wins loses progress, so fields need per-field rules — union for sets, max for XP — chosen from what each field means.
When would you NOT enable offline persistence?
For data that must never be stale or stored on the device — shared admin dashboards, sensitive records — or where cache size and multi-tab behaviour add risk without benefit.

lessons.sub: Rules are your backend — write them like code, test them like code
lessons.goal: By the end you can write Firestore security rules that enforce owner-only access, validate data shapes on write, use cross-document lookups safely, and explain why rules are not filters.
lessons.body:
1. Rules decide every request, allow or deny

Firestore security rules run on Google's servers for every read and write. There is no way around them from a client: if the rules deny it, the data does not move. A rule is a match on a path plus an allow condition. The most important pattern in Skillzify is owner-only access — a signed-in user may read and write only the document whose ID equals their own user ID — which makes the database itself enforce the privacy boundary instead of trusting every client to behave.

2. Validate the shape, not just the identity

Rules can inspect the incoming data, so you can require that XP is a number, that a lesson ID is a string, or that a profile name is under 50 characters. This turns rules into a server-side schema check: a buggy or malicious client cannot write a string where a number belongs, even though it controls the code that sends the write. Keep the checks cheap — every get call inside a rule is a billed read, and rules have a time limit.

3. Rules are not filters

The rule that trips up every beginner: rules cannot hide documents inside a query result. If a query could return a document the rules deny, the whole query fails — Firestore does not silently filter it out. So queries must be written to match the rules: ask only for documents the requester is allowed to see. Design the rules and the queries together, as one system, and test both with the rules emulator before publishing.

rules_version = '2';
service cloud.firestore {
  match /databases/{database}/documents {
    match /users/{uid} {
      allow read, write: if request.auth != null
        && request.auth.uid == uid
        && request.resource.data.xp is int
        && request.resource.data.xp >= 0;
    }
    match /questions/{qid} {
      allow read: if true;
      allow create: if request.auth != null
        && request.resource.data.authorId == request.auth.uid;
      allow delete: if request.auth != null
        && resource.data.authorId == request.auth.uid;
    }
  }
}

Notice the two data objects: request.resource.data is the incoming write, resource.data is the existing document. Confusing them is the most common rules bug.
lessons.task: Write rules for a new Skillzify feature — public showcase posts that anyone can read, only the author can delete, and only signed-in users can create with their own authorId. Test all four cases (anonymous read, anonymous create, author delete, stranger delete) in the Firestore rules emulator, and fix every failure before publishing.
checks: Why does a query fail entirely instead of returning only the allowed documents?
Rules are not filters. If a query could match a denied document, Firestore rejects the whole query — queries must be scoped to documents the requester may read.
What is the difference between resource.data and request.resource.data?
resource.data is the document already stored; request.resource.data is the document as it would look after the write being checked.
interview: A rule uses get() to check another document — what is the cost and the risk?
Each get() is a billed read and adds latency, and rules have evaluation limits. Overusing cross-document lookups makes rules slow, expensive and fragile.
How do you prove rules are correct before real users depend on them?
Unit-test them with the Firestore rules emulator: scripted allow and deny cases for every role, run in CI, and never publish untested rule edits.

lessons.sub: Denormalise on purpose, fan out on write, and know when to stop
lessons.goal: By the end you can choose between embedding and subcollections, design a fan-out write, handle counters that many users update at once, and spot the modelling smell that says a design will not scale.
lessons.body:
1. Embed or subcollection: the one question

Every modelling decision in Firestore reduces to one question: is this data bounded and always read with its parent? If yes, embed it in the document. A user profile, streak record and settings live inside users/{uid} because they are small and always loaded together. If the data grows without bound — every question a user ever asked, every event ever logged — it belongs in a subcollection, where it can be queried and paginated independently. An array that grows forever will eventually hit the 1 MiB document limit, and that failure arrives suddenly in production.

2. Denormalise on purpose

NoSQL modelling accepts duplication as the price of fast reads. If the community list shows each question with its author's display name, storing the name on the question document avoids a second read per question. The cost is maintenance: when a user changes their name, every copy must update. That is a fan-out write — one user action updates many documents — and it belongs in a Cloud Function or a batched write, never in code the user can skip.

3. Counters and hot documents

A single counter document that every learner increments — total lessons completed across the site — becomes a hot document: Firestore allows roughly one write per second per document, and concurrent increments start failing. The fix is sharded counters: spread increments across ten counter documents and sum them on read. It is more code, but it is the difference between a feature that works for ten users and one that works for ten thousand.

// Sharded counter: pick a shard at random on write, sum on read
const SHARDS = 10;
async function incrementCounter(db, counterId) {
  const shard = Math.floor(Math.random() * SHARDS);
  const ref = doc(db, "counters", counterId + "_" + shard);
  await setDoc(ref, { count: increment(1) }, { merge: true });
}
// Read: fetch all 10 shard docs and add their count fields.

The same idea applies anywhere many writers hit one document: spread the writes, aggregate on read.
lessons.task: Design the data model for Skillzify's weekly featured showcase: a list page showing post title, author name and star count, plus a detail page with comments. Decide what is embedded, what is a subcollection, where the author name is duplicated, and how the star counter avoids becoming a hot document. Write the model as a short document with a reason for each choice.
checks: When should data go in a subcollection instead of inside the parent document?
When it grows without bound or needs independent querying and pagination — embedding it would eventually hit the 1 MiB document limit.
Why do high-traffic counters use shards instead of one document?
One document accepts roughly one write per second. Shards spread concurrent writes across many documents, and the total is summed on read.
interview: Your user changes their display name. What breaks if you denormalised it onto their posts?
Every copy is stale until a fan-out write updates it. You need a reliable update path — a Cloud Function or batched write — or you accept showing the old name.
How do you decide what to denormalise?
By read patterns: duplicate the fields a list view needs so it renders in one query, and only where the update cost of keeping copies fresh is acceptable.

lessons.sub: The two ideas that make relational databases worth learning
lessons.goal: By the end you can write INNER and LEFT JOINs, use GROUP BY with COUNT, SUM and AVG, filter groups with HAVING, and translate a Skillzify Firestore model into tables with foreign keys.
lessons.body:
1. Joins stitch tables at read time

SQL stores data normalised — one fact in one place — and reassembles it when you ask. An INNER JOIN returns only rows that match on both sides: lessons joined to their completions give you only lessons someone finished. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table even when there is no match, so you can list all lessons with a completion count that is zero for untouched ones. That difference is the single most-tested SQL idea, and it maps directly to a question Firestore cannot answer at all: show me everything, including the things with no activity.

2. Aggregates answer questions about groups

COUNT, SUM and AVG collapse many rows into one number, and GROUP BY runs them per group instead of for the whole table: total XP per user, average quiz score per section, lessons completed per day. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after — users with more than 100 XP, sections averaging below 50 percent. Mixing those two up is the classic aggregate mistake, and interviewers ask it precisely because it reveals whether you understand the order SQL executes in.

3. The same schema, two shapes

Skillzify's users/{uid} document becomes a users table plus a completions table with a foreign key back to the user, and an exercises table keyed by user and exercise. Nothing is duplicated: the display name lives in one row. The price is that every read is now a join, and every new question needs a new query — the exact trade-off Firestore made in the opposite direction. Neither shape is correct in general; the right one follows from your read patterns.

-- Average quiz score per section, only for sections with 5+ attempts
SELECT section, AVG(score) AS avg_score, COUNT(*) AS attempts
FROM quiz_attempts
GROUP BY section
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY avg_score ASC;

-- All lessons with completions, including never-attempted ones
SELECT l.title, COUNT(c.user_id) AS completions
FROM lessons l
LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.lesson_id = l.id
GROUP BY l.id, l.title;

Read the second query out loud: lessons are the left side, completions may or may not exist, and COUNT of the joined key is zero when nothing matched — that is the LEFT JOIN doing its job.
lessons.task: Create two SQLite tables — lessons(id, title, section) and completions(user_id, lesson_id) — with 6 lessons and 8 completion rows. Write three queries: lessons never completed by anyone (LEFT JOIN with a null check), completions per section, and sections averaging fewer than 2 completions per lesson. Check each result by hand against the raw rows.
checks: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills unmatched columns with null.
WHERE vs HAVING — which filters groups, and why does the order matter?
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation; WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, so it cannot use aggregate results.
interview: Why does SQL normalise while Firestore denormalises?

SQL is built for ad-hoc questions answered at read time with joins, so one copy of each fact is best. Firestore is built for planned reads with no joins, so data is duplicated to make each read cheap.
A query is slow on a large table. What do you check first?
Whether the filtered and joined columns are indexed, and the query plan — a missing index turns a lookup into a full table scan.

lessons.sub: Two databases, two answers to the question: who may do what?
lessons.goal: By the end you can compare Firestore security rules with SQL grants and row-level security, explain where each system enforces access, and choose the right model for a given feature.
lessons.body:
1. Firestore: rules travel with the data

In Firestore, access control is a program attached to the database. Rules evaluate on every request, using the caller's identity and the document's contents, and there is no separate application server in the path to bypass them — the client talks to Firestore directly. That is powerful and dangerous in equal measure: a rule mistake is a live security hole, and there is no middleware to catch what the rules miss. Owner-only access, validation of incoming shapes, and the rules-are-not-filters principle from Lesson 4.6 are the whole game.

2. SQL: grants, then row-level security

Relational databases split access into two layers. GRANT controls which tables and operations a database role may touch at all — the application role can select from lessons but never delete from users. Row-level security goes further: a policy on a table filters which rows a role can see, so a learner's query transparently returns only their own rows. The crucial difference from Firestore is where enforcement sits: SQL expects an application server between the user and the database, so policies usually protect against application bugs and insider access rather than against a hostile client holding the keys.

3. Choosing between the models

Use Firestore rules when clients talk directly to the database and access is mostly per-user and document-shaped — exactly Skillzify's case. Use SQL grants and row-level security when an application server owns the data access and you need complex, cross-table access logic or audit trails. A hybrid is common: Firestore for user-scoped app data, Postgres for reporting and admin data that no client ever touches directly. The question is never which system is more secure in the abstract — it is which enforcement point matches your architecture.

-- Postgres row-level security: a learner sees only their own rows
ALTER TABLE completions ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY learner_own_rows ON completions
  FOR ALL
  USING (user_id = current_setting('app.current_user_id'));

-- Firestore equivalent, for comparison:
-- allow read, write: if request.auth != null
--   && request.auth.uid == uid;

Both snippets express the same idea — you may touch only your own data — but one runs inside a database your server controls, and the other runs on a database your client talks to directly.
lessons.task: Take Skillzify's owner-only Firestore rule and rewrite it as a Postgres row-level security policy on a completions table. Then list three access requirements that are easy in one system and awkward in the other — for example, a teacher who may read every student in their class — and say which system you would pick for each.
checks: Where does Firestore enforce access, and where does SQL usually enforce it?
Firestore rules run on the database for direct client requests; SQL access is usually enforced behind an application server, with grants and row-level security as a second layer.
Why is a Firestore rule mistake more dangerous than a SQL grant mistake?
Clients talk to Firestore directly with no server in between, so a permissive rule is immediately exploitable by anyone. A SQL mistake is usually shielded by the application server.
interview: When would you put row-level security in Postgres instead of checking ownership in application code?
When the guarantee must hold no matter which code path queries the table — reporting jobs, admin tools, future services — so the database itself is the last line of defence.
Your app needs a teacher to read all students in their class. How does that change each model?

In Firestore it needs a rule that looks up the teacher's class membership, costing a get per request; in SQL it is a policy joining the class roster table — both work, but the cost and complexity land in different places.

lessons.sub: The unit everything in LLM pricing and prompting is measured in
lessons.goal: By the end you can estimate the token cost of a prompt, explain why the same text costs different tokens in different models, and design prompts that fit a context window instead of overflowing it.
lessons.body:
1. What a token actually is

A token is a chunk of text — roughly three quarters of an English word on average. The model never sees words or letters; it sees token IDs produced by a tokenizer that splits text by frequency, so common words become one token and rare words splinter into several. That is why counting characters is a poor estimate of cost: the same sentence can cost different tokens depending on the words in it, and code, with its symbols and indentation, tokenizes far less efficiently than prose. Every price, limit and quota in the LLM world is denominated in tokens, so this unit is the budget you actually manage.

2. The context window is a hard wall

The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can consider in one request — prompt plus reply combined. Exceed it and the request fails outright; there is no graceful overflow. Gemini's large windows invite a lazy habit — paste everything — which costs money on every call and degrades answer quality, because the model attends less precisely to any one fact when the window is stuffed. The disciplined move is to send the smallest context that answers the question: a retrieved lesson excerpt, not the whole curriculum.

3. Counting before you send

Count tokens before the call, not after the bill. Gemini's countTokens endpoint exists precisely for this, and Skillzify's server should use it to enforce caps before spending anything. Rough mental math works too: about 4 characters per token for English, worse for code. Track three numbers per feature — tokens in, tokens out, and cost per call — and every pricing or cap decision becomes arithmetic instead of guesswork.

// Estimate and enforce before spending: count, then cap
const count = await model.countTokens({
  contents: [{ role: "user", parts: [{ text: prompt }] }]
});
console.log("prompt tokens:", count.totalTokens);

if (count.totalTokens > 8000) {
  prompt = summariseOrTruncate(prompt); // never send blind
}
// Rule of thumb: ~4 chars per token for English, ~2-3 for code.

Output tokens cost more than input tokens on most models, so a rambling reply is also a budget line — ask for concise formats and set max output tokens per mode.
lessons.task: Take three real Skillzify tutor prompts — a short hint request, a lesson explanation, and a full-lesson paste — and count their tokens with the countTokens endpoint. Record input tokens, estimated cost, and how much of a 1M-token window each uses. Then rewrite the full-lesson prompt to use a retrieved excerpt instead, and measure the saving.
checks: Why is character count a bad way to estimate token cost?
Tokenizers split by frequency: common words are one token, rare words and code splinter into several, so identical lengths can cost very different token counts.
What happens when prompt plus reply exceed the context window?
The request fails. There is no graceful overflow, so you must count and trim before sending.
interview: How do you keep LLM costs predictable in a product with free users?
Count tokens before each call, enforce per-user daily caps server-side, prefer small retrieved context over full-document pastes, and cap output tokens per mode.
Why does stuffing the context window hurt answer quality, not just cost?
Attention dilutes: with more context the model weighs any single fact less precisely, so long prompts often produce vaguer answers than focused ones.

lessons.sub: Make the model return JSON you can trust, and show it arriving live
lessons.goal: By the end you can force Gemini to return valid JSON matching a schema, stream a response token by token to the UI, and handle the partial-JSON problem that streaming creates.
lessons.body:
1. Structured output: a contract, not a hope

Asking a model to reply in JSON with a polite instruction works until it does not — one day it adds a chatty sentence before the brace and your JSON.parse throws. Structured output turns the format into a contract: you declare a response schema, set the MIME type to JSON, and the model is constrained to produce only valid JSON matching that schema. Skillzify's quiz generator uses this to get exactly three questions, each with four options and one correct index — fields the frontend can render without defensive parsing gymnastics.

2. Streaming: show work as it arrives

A normal API call waits for the full reply, which can take seconds of dead silence. Streaming returns the response in chunks as tokens are generated, so the UI can render words as they appear — the typing effect users expect from AI chat. Under the hood it is server-sent events: the server forwards chunks, the client appends them. The cost is complexity: your UI now has three states — streaming, done, and failed halfway — and each needs handling.

3. The partial-JSON problem

Streaming and structured output collide: while streaming, the JSON is incomplete, so you cannot parse it until the final chunk. The standard solution is to stream the raw text for display and parse only the completed string, or to design the schema so each field can render progressively. Never render a half-parsed object as if it were final — a question with two options and no answer key is worse than a loading spinner.

// Structured output: schema-enforced JSON from Gemini
const result = await model.generateContent({
  contents: [{ role: "user", parts: [{ text: quizPrompt }] }],
  generationConfig: {
    responseMimeType: "application/json",
    responseSchema: {
      type: "OBJECT",
      properties: {
        question: { type: "STRING" },
        options: { type: "ARRAY", items: { type: "STRING" } },
        answerIndex: { type: "INTEGER" }
      },
      required: ["question", "options", "answerIndex"]
    }
  }
});
const quiz = JSON.parse(result.response.text()); // guaranteed valid JSON

Streaming uses generateContentStream and iterates the stream, appending each chunk's text. Same schema, same guarantee — only the delivery changes.
lessons.task: Build a quiz-question generator endpoint that returns structured JSON with the schema above for any lesson topic. Call it once normally and once with streaming, logging the time to first chunk versus time to complete response. Then deliberately break the schema by removing a required field and confirm the model still returns valid JSON matching the new schema.
checks: Why is a response schema better than asking for JSON in the prompt text?
The schema constrains generation itself, so the output is guaranteed valid JSON in the declared shape. A prompt instruction is a suggestion the model can ignore or decorate.
Why can you not parse streamed JSON until the stream finishes?
Mid-stream the JSON is incomplete and invalid. You stream raw text for display and parse only the completed string.
interview: When would you choose streaming over a single response?
For long, user-facing text where perceived latency matters — chat, explanations — because first tokens arrive in under a second. For machine-consumed JSON, a single call is simpler.
How do you handle a streamed response that fails halfway?
Keep the partial text visible with a clear incomplete state, offer retry, and never persist or act on the partial structured result as if it were complete.

lessons.sub: Give the model hands: declare tools, run them, return the result
lessons.goal: By the end you can declare a function tool for Gemini, handle the model's functionCall response, execute the real function, feed the result back, and explain the loop that makes agents work.
lessons.body:
1. The model does not run code — it asks you to

Tool calling is the most misunderstood LLM feature. The model never executes your function. It reads the tool declaration — name, description, parameters — decides the user's request needs that tool, and returns a structured function call: which function, with which arguments. Your code runs the function against the real world, then sends the result back to the model, which writes the final answer. The model is the brain that decides; your server is the hands that act.

2. The loop, step by step

One turn becomes a loop: send the prompt plus tool declarations; if the reply contains a function call, execute it and append the result as a function-response message; send the conversation back and repeat until the model answers in plain text. Skillzify's tutor could offer a getLessonProgress tool — the learner asks where they stand, the model calls the tool, your server reads Firestore, and the model turns the raw numbers into a human answer. The tool's description is its documentation to the model: vague descriptions produce wrong calls.

3. Trust boundaries matter

Tools that read are safe to expose broadly; tools that write need gates. A tool that marks a lesson complete or changes XP must validate the caller and the arguments server-side, because the model can be tricked by prompt injection in user input into calling tools with attacker-chosen arguments. Treat every function call like an API request from an untrusted client: validate, authorise, then execute.

// Declare the tool, then run the loop
const tools = [{ functionDeclarations: [{ name: "getLessonProgress",
  description: "Return the learner's completed lessons, XP and streak.",
  parameters: { type: "OBJECT", properties: {
    uid: { type: "STRING", description: "The learner's user id" } } }
}] }];

const res = await model.generateContent({ contents: chat, tools });
const call = res.response.functionCalls?.()[0];
if (call) {
  const data = await runTool(call.name, call.args); // YOUR code runs it
  chat.push({ role: "function", parts: [{ functionResponse: { name: call.name, response: data } }] });
  const final = await model.generateContent({ contents: chat, tools });
}

One declaration, one executor, one loop — that pattern scales from one tool to twenty, and it is the entire machinery behind AI agents.
lessons.task: Add a getLessonProgress tool to the Skillzify tutor backend: declare it, implement the executor against Firestore, and wire the two-turn loop. Test with the prompt 'How am I doing this week?' and verify the final answer uses real numbers from your database, not invented ones. Then add a second read-only tool of your own choosing.
checks: Who actually executes a function the model calls?
Your server code. The model only returns a structured call request; you run the function and send the result back for the final answer.
Why do write tools need server-side validation even though the model chose the arguments?
Arguments can be influenced by prompt injection in user input, so every call must be validated and authorised like any untrusted API request.
interview: Explain the tool-calling loop in one minute.
Declare tools with schemas, send prompt plus declarations, execute any returned function call, append the result, repeat until the model answers in text.
What makes a good tool description?
Precise purpose, when to use it, what each parameter means and its constraints — the description is the model's only documentation, so vagueness causes wrong calls.

lessons.sub: Retrieval that scales, and caching that cuts the bill
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain embeddings and cosine similarity, design a chunk-and-retrieve pipeline for Skillzify's lessons, and use prompt caching to stop paying for the same context on every call.
lessons.body:
1. Embeddings turn meaning into geometry

An embedding is a list of numbers — a vector — produced from a piece of text, positioned so that similar meanings sit close together. Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors: near 1 means near-identical meaning, near 0 means unrelated. A vector database stores these embeddings alongside the original text and answers one question fast: given this query vector, which stored vectors are closest? That is the retrieval half of RAG, and it is how a tutor can find the three most relevant lesson passages for a question instead of pasting the whole course into the prompt.

2. Chunking decides retrieval quality

You do not embed whole lessons. You split them into chunks — a section, a paragraph, a concept — because a query matches a focused chunk far more precisely than a long document that mentions everything. Too small and the chunk lacks context; too large and it dilutes the match. Overlap the chunks slightly so an idea split across a boundary is still retrievable, and store metadata — lesson ID, section — so the retrieved text can link back to its source instead of floating as an uncited claim.

3. Prompt caching: pay once for repeated context

Many calls share the same long prefix — the system prompt, the course outline, the retrieved passages. Prompt caching stores that prefix server-side and charges a fraction for reusing it instead of reprocessing it every time. Gemini's context caching works the same way: cache the stable context, send only the new question per call. The saving is real money at volume, and the design rule is simple — keep the stable part stable and put the changing part last.

// RAG in five lines of intent: embed, search, build, ask
const qVec = await embed(question);               // query -> vector
const hits = await vectorDb.search(qVec, { topK: 3 }); // nearest chunks
const context = hits.map(h => h.text).join("\n---\n");
const answer = await model.generateContent(
  "Answer using only this context:\n" + context + "\n\nQ: " + question);
// Cache the stable system prompt + outline once; send only the question.

Retrieval quality is the product's quality: bad chunks mean confident answers from the wrong passage, so evaluate retrieval separately from generation.
lessons.task: Build a tiny RAG demo over five Skillzify lesson texts: chunk each lesson into sections, embed the chunks with Gemini's embedding model, store them in an in-memory list, and answer three test questions by cosine similarity retrieval plus generation. Then cache the shared system prompt with context caching and measure the token saving across ten calls.
checks: What does cosine similarity measure between two embedding vectors?
The angle between them: near 1 means the texts are semantically close, near 0 means unrelated — it is the ranking signal for retrieval.
Why chunk documents instead of embedding whole lessons?
A focused chunk matches a query precisely; a whole lesson dilutes the match and returns vague context. Chunks also keep retrieved context small and cheap.
interview: RAG vs fine-tuning vs a long prompt — when is each right?
RAG for knowledge that changes or must be cited; fine-tuning for stable style or behaviour; long prompts only for small, one-off context.
How do you know your retrieval is bad before users complain?
Evaluate it separately: a test set of questions with known-correct source chunks, measuring whether the right chunk is in the top results.

lessons.sub: Ship AI you can defend: block the bad, measure the rest
lessons.goal: By the end you can name the guardrails each Skillzify AI mode needs, build a small eval set with golden answers, run it after a prompt change, and decide from the numbers whether the change ships.
lessons.body:
1. Guardrails: input, output, and action

Guardrails sit in three places. Input guardrails check the prompt before the model sees it: block prompt-injection attempts, cap length, reject disallowed requests early. Output guardrails check the reply before the user sees it: enforce format, strip anything off-topic, catch hallucinations in structured fields like answer indexes that point at nonexistent options. Action guardrails gate what tools may do — a tutor may read progress but never write XP. Gemini's built-in safety settings cover the broad harms; your own guardrails cover the product-specific failures, which are the ones users actually hit.

2. Evals: a test suite for behaviour

You cannot improve what you do not measure, and AI behaviour is not covered by unit tests. An eval set is a list of inputs with expected outputs — golden answers — for one feature: twenty tutor questions with correct answers, ten quiz generations with verifiable answer keys. Run the set, score the outputs, and you get a number. Change the prompt, run it again, and the number tells you whether you helped or hurt. Without evals, prompt tuning is superstition: every change feels better because you only remember the examples that improved.

3. The loop that makes AI reliable

Collect real failures from production logs, add them to the eval set, fix the prompt or the guardrail, re-run, and ship only when the score holds or improves. Review the worst outputs by hand every week — automated scoring misses the plausible-sounding wrong answer that a human spots in seconds. This is the unglamorous work that separates a demo from a product learners can trust with their exam preparation.

// Minimal eval runner: prompt, expected, score — then decide
const evalSet = [
  { q: "What is a closure?", mustContain: ["function", "scope"] },
  { q: "Explain Big-O of binary search", mustContain: ["log"] }
];
let pass = 0;
for (const item of evalSet) {
  const out = await askTutor(item.q);
  const ok = item.mustContain.every(w => out.toLowerCase().includes(w));
  if (ok) pass++;
  console.log(ok ? "PASS" : "FAIL", "-", item.q);
}
console.log("score:", pass + "/" + evalSet.length);

Start with keyword checks; graduate to a model-graded rubric only when keyword checks can no longer tell good from bad.
lessons.task: Build an eval set of 10 questions for the Skillzify tutor with golden answers you verify by hand. Run it against the current prompt, record the score, then make one prompt change and re-run. Write a one-paragraph ship or no-ship decision based on the numbers, and add the two worst failures to the eval set as regression cases.
checks: What is the difference between a guardrail and an eval?
A guardrail blocks or fixes bad behaviour at runtime; an eval measures behaviour offline so you know whether a change helped before it ships.
Why must every production AI failure become an eval case?
So the same failure is caught automatically next time. Without regression cases, prompt fixes silently re-break.
interview: How do you evaluate a tutor's answers when there is no single correct wording?
With a rubric: required concepts, forbidden errors, and a small human-graded sample — keyword checks for structure, human review for substance.
A prompt change improves 8 eval cases and breaks 2. Ship it?
Only if the 2 are less important than the 8 and you understand why they broke. Otherwise fix the regression first — evals exist to stop trading one failure for another.

lessons.sub: Real Python in the browser: workers, packages, and the JS bridge
lessons.goal: By the end you can load Pyodide in a Web Worker, run user code with captured stdout, install packages with micropip, and pass data between Python and JavaScript without freezing the page.
lessons.body:
1. Pyodide is CPython compiled to WebAssembly

Pyodide is the real CPython interpreter, compiled to WebAssembly so it runs entirely in the browser — no server, no sandbox account, no per-run cost. That is why Skillzify's Code Studio can run learner code instantly and offline: the runtime downloads once, then every run is local. The trade-off is size and startup time — the runtime is several megabytes — so you load it once, lazily, and show honest loading state instead of pretending it is instant.

2. Run it in a Worker, never on the main thread

Python code can loop forever, and a loop on the main thread freezes the whole page. The fix is a Web Worker: Pyodide lives in a separate thread, the UI stays responsive, and you can terminate the worker when code runs too long. Communication is message-passing — the main thread sends code, the worker sends back output, errors and a done signal. Skillzify's compiler is this architecture: the editor is the UI, the worker is the machine.

3. The bridge: stdout, packages, and data

Three bridge details make it feel like a real environment. First, capture stdout by redirecting Python's print output into a buffer the worker returns as text. Second, install packages with micropip — loadPackage for the bundled scientific stack, micropip.install for pure-Python packages from PyPI — and cache them so the second run is fast. Third, move data across the bridge with toJs and fromJs: Python lists become JS arrays, dicts become Maps, and proxies must be destroyed or they leak memory.

// Inside the worker: load once, run many times
importScripts("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/v0.26.4/full/pyodide.js");
let pyodideReady = loadPyodide();

onmessage = async (e) => {
  const pyodide = await pyodideReady;
  pyodide.setStdout({ batched: (s) => postMessage({ type: "out", text: s }) });
  try {
    await pyodide.loadPackage("numpy"); // or micropip.install("requests")
    const result = await pyodide.runPythonAsync(e.data.code);
    postMessage({ type: "done", result: String(result) });
  } catch (err) {
    postMessage({ type: "error", text: String(err.message) });
  }
};
// Main thread: new Worker("pyodide-worker.js"), post code, kill on timeout.

Guard the worker with a timeout — terminate and respawn after a few seconds — because an infinite loop has no other off switch.
lessons.task: Build a single-page Pyodide runner: a textarea, a Run button, and an output pane, with Pyodide in a Web Worker and a 5-second timeout that kills and respawns the worker. Verify three things: print output appears, an infinite loop freezes nothing, and import numpy works after loadPackage.
checks: Why must Pyodide run in a Web Worker instead of the main thread?
Python code can loop forever; on the main thread that freezes the page. A worker keeps the UI responsive and can be terminated on timeout.
How do you get print output out of Pyodide and into your page?
Redirect Python stdout with setStdout and forward each batch to the main thread as a message, which appends it to the output pane.
interview: Pyodide vs running Python on a server — when is each right?
Pyodide for instant, free, offline-capable runs of learner code; a server for untrusted code at scale, heavy packages, or work that must not depend on the user's device.
What leaks if you pass Python objects to JavaScript carelessly?
PyProxy objects wrap Python values; if you never destroy them they hold Python objects alive and leak memory. Convert with toJs or destroy the proxy.

lessons.sub: Beyond a textarea: highlighting, completion, lint and themes
lessons.goal: By the end you can assemble a CodeMirror 6 editor from extensions, add Python highlighting and autocompletion, wire a lint source, and explain why extensions compose instead of inheriting.
lessons.body:
1. CodeMirror 6 is a box of composable extensions

CodeMirror 6 is not one editor with settings — it is a small core plus extensions that each add one capability: line numbers, syntax highlighting, autocompletion, search, themes. You build an editor by listing the extensions you want, and two editors can share most of a list while differing in one piece. That composition model is why Skillzify can use the same editor for the Python runner and the flowchart code view with different language support: same core, different extension lists.

2. Language support is a data package

Syntax highlighting comes from a language package — @codemirror/lang-python for Python — which parses the code and tags each token so a theme can colour it. Autocompletion is a separate extension that suggests identifiers as you type, fed by a completion source you can extend with Skillzify's own lesson vocabulary. The key insight is that highlighting is parsing: the editor genuinely understands the code's structure, which is why it can also bracket-match, fold blocks and indent correctly.

3. Linting: your own diagnostics, live

The lint extension shows squiggles under problems, driven by a lint source — a function that receives the document and returns diagnostics with positions and severities. You can wire it to Pyodide: run a syntax check on each edit and surface Python's own error messages in the editor, at the exact line. That closes the loop between writing and running: the editor stops being a fancy textarea and becomes a small IDE.

import { EditorView, basicSetup } from "codemirror";
import { python } from "@codemirror/lang-python";
import { autocompletion } from "@codemirror/autocomplete";
import { linter } from "@codemirror/lint";

const view = new EditorView({
  doc: "print('hello')\n",
  extensions: [
    basicSetup,
    python(),
    autocompletion(),
    linter(async (view) => checkWithPyodide(view.state.doc.toString()))
  ],
  parent: document.getElementById("editor")
});

Extensions are values in an array — swap one, and the editor's behaviour changes without touching anything else. That is the whole design philosophy in one line.
lessons.task: Build a CodeMirror 6 editor for Python with highlighting, autocompletion and a lint source that flags lines longer than 79 characters. Then add a second editor instance on the same page for JavaScript, sharing the base extension list, and note exactly which extensions differ and why.
checks: Why does CodeMirror 6 use extensions instead of configuration flags?
Extensions compose: each adds one capability, so editors share most of a list and differ in one piece, instead of inheriting a fixed feature set.
What does a lint source receive and return?
It receives the editor view and document, and returns diagnostics — each with a position, severity and message — which the editor renders as squiggles.
interview: How would you add Skillzify lesson keywords to autocompletion?
Write a custom completion source that merges the language's completions with your own list, and register it as an extension alongside the default one.
Highlighting looks cosmetic — why is it actually parsing?
Because the language package tokenises the code structurally, which is what also enables bracket matching, folding and correct indentation. Colour is the visible side effect.

lessons.sub: Subgraphs, styling, interaction — diagrams that behave like UI
lessons.goal: By the end you can write Mermaid diagrams with subgraphs and custom styles, make nodes clickable, handle render errors gracefully, and choose the right diagram type for the idea.
lessons.body:
1. Subgraphs group ideas, styles direct the eye

A flat flowchart of twenty nodes is unreadable; subgraphs fix that by grouping related nodes into labelled boxes — input, processing, output — so the reader sees structure before detail. Styling goes further: class definitions colour nodes by role, so decision points, errors and success paths are recognisable at a glance. Skillzify's flowchart generator emits subgraphs for function boundaries and colours error paths differently, which is why generated diagrams stay readable as programs grow.

2. Diagrams can be interactive

Mermaid nodes support click bindings: a node can link to a URL or trigger a callback. In Skillzify that means a flowchart node can jump to the lesson that explains the concept it represents — the diagram becomes navigation, not just a picture. Direction matters too: top-to-bottom suits processes, left-to-right suits timelines, and switching direction is one word in the diagram source. When a diagram renders badly, the fix is usually direction or grouping, not more nodes.

3. Render failures are a product problem

Mermaid parses a text syntax, and invalid syntax fails at render time — in front of the user. Never let a render error become a blank page: catch the failure, show the offending line, and keep the source visible so it can be fixed. Security level matters as well: Mermaid's default settings can execute embedded interaction, so Skillzify renders with a strict security level and sanitises generated source before it ever reaches the renderer.

flowchart TD
  subgraph Input
    A[Read code] --> B[Parse to AST]
  end
  subgraph Output
    B --> C[Build JSON]
    C --> D[Render diagram]
  end
  B --> E[Syntax error]
  classDef error fill:#7f1d1d,color:#fff;
  class E error;
  click D "https://skillzify.example.com/lessons/mermaid" "Open the lesson"

One diagram source, three powers: structure from subgraphs, meaning from classes, and behaviour from click bindings.
lessons.task: Write a Mermaid flowchart for the Skillzify flowchart pipeline — Python code in, JSON in the middle, diagram out — using two subgraphs, one styled error node, and a click binding on the render node. Then deliberately break the syntax, confirm your page shows a helpful error with the source intact, and fix it.
checks: When should you use subgraphs instead of adding more nodes to a flat diagram?
When nodes form natural groups — input, processing, output — so the reader sees structure before detail and the diagram stays readable at twenty-plus nodes.
Why must Mermaid render errors be caught and shown, not left blank?
A blank page hides the problem. Showing the error and the source lets the user fix the one broken line instead of guessing.
interview: Flowchart, sequence diagram, class diagram — how do you choose?
By what you need to show: control flow, interaction over time, or static structure. The idea picks the diagram, not the other way round.
Why does rendering user-generated Mermaid need a strict security level?
Mermaid can bind interactions from diagram source, so untrusted source could inject behaviour. Strict mode and sanitisation keep diagrams pictures, not code.

lessons.sub: DevTools is the debugger — breakpoints, scopes, and the network tab
lessons.goal: By the end you can set breakpoints and conditional breakpoints, inspect scope and the call stack, debug a failing fetch in the Network tab, and reproduce a bug before fixing it.
lessons.body:
1. Breakpoints beat console.log

Scattering console.log calls tells you what happened at points you guessed in advance. A breakpoint stops execution exactly where you choose, and while paused you can inspect every variable in scope, hover expressions, and step line by line. Conditional breakpoints go further: pause only when the lesson ID equals the broken one, or when the counter passes one hundred — invaluable when a bug appears once in a thousand iterations. The debugger statement in code does the same thing from the source: when DevTools is open, execution pauses there.

2. The call stack tells you how you got here

When paused, the call stack shows the chain of function calls that led to this line. That is usually where the bug lives — not in the line that threw, but in the caller that passed the wrong value three frames up. The Scope panel shows local variables, closures and globals side by side, so you can see which value is wrong and where it came from. Watch expressions pin the values you care about across steps, so you notice the moment one goes wrong.

3. The Network tab debugs the backend you cannot see

Half of frontend bugs are not in the frontend. The Network tab shows every request: its URL, status, headers, payload and response, with timing. A tutor call that returns nothing is diagnosed here in seconds — wrong endpoint, missing auth header, a 500 with an error body, a CORS rejection. Pair it with the Console for errors and the Application tab for localStorage and IndexedDB, and most Skillzify bugs become visible before you touch any code.

// The three debugging moves, in order:
// 1. Reproduce it reliably — same steps, same result, every time.
// 2. Pause it: set a breakpoint, or add this line where it breaks:
debugger; // pauses here when DevTools is open
// 3. Inspect: Scope panel for values, Call Stack for how you got here,
//    Network tab for what the server actually returned.

Rule of the craft: reproduce first, fix second. A fix for a bug you cannot reproduce is a guess you cannot verify.
lessons.task: Take the Skillzify lesson page and plant a real bug: make the Next Up card show the wrong lesson by passing a stale progress object. Reproduce it, set a conditional breakpoint that pauses only for that lesson, walk the call stack to the caller that passed the stale data, fix it, and confirm the breakpoint no longer triggers.
checks: Why is a conditional breakpoint better than a plain one in a loop that runs a thousand times?
It pauses only when the condition matches — the one broken iteration — instead of forcing you to step through 999 correct ones.
A fetch returns nothing useful. Which DevTools tab diagnoses it first, and what do you look for?
The Network tab: the request's status, payload and response body show whether the endpoint, headers or server reply is wrong.
interview: Walk me through debugging a bug you cannot reproduce on your machine.
Reproduce with the user's exact steps and data, add logging at the boundaries, check environment differences like cached files or auth state, and bisect recent changes.
When do you use console.log anyway, despite having a debugger?
For async flows and timing issues where pausing changes the behaviour, and for quick traces across many events where breakpoints would be too slow.

lessons.sub: Measure first: long tasks, layout thrash, and the bundle that ate the page
lessons.goal: By the end you can record a Performance trace, identify long tasks and layout thrash, run Lighthouse and act on its findings, and explain INP in one sentence.
lessons.body:
1. Measure, then optimise — never the reverse

Performance work without measurement is superstition. The Performance panel records what the browser actually does — scripting, rendering, painting — on a timeline you can inspect frame by frame. A long task is any JavaScript block over 50 milliseconds, and it is what users feel as a frozen button or a stuttering scroll. The first trace usually surprises: the slow part is rarely the code you suspected. Skillzify's lesson list rendering, for example, is fast — the expensive part is usually a third-party script or an oversized image nobody measured.

2. The usual suspects

Four patterns cause most slowness. Long tasks block the main thread — split them with chunking or move them to a worker, exactly as Pyodide already is. Layout thrash happens when code reads a layout value then writes a style in a loop, forcing the browser to recalculate layout every iteration — batch reads, then batch writes. Oversized images and fonts delay first paint — serve sized images and preload only the font weights you use. And a large JavaScript bundle delays interactivity — load Pyodide and CodeMirror lazily, only on the pages that need them.

3. Lighthouse and real-user metrics

Lighthouse gives a lab score and a prioritised list — it is a starting point, not a verdict. The numbers that matter in production are the Core Web Vitals: how fast the largest content paints, how much the layout shifts, and INP — Interaction to Next Paint — how quickly the page responds to a tap. INP is the one users feel most directly: a button that takes 300 milliseconds to respond feels broken, whatever the Lighthouse score says.

// Find long tasks in the wild, not just in the lab
const observer = new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (entry.duration > 50) {
      console.warn("Long task:", Math.round(entry.duration), "ms");
    }
  }
});
observer.observe({ entryTypes: ["longtask"] });
// Fix order: split the work, defer non-critical scripts, batch DOM writes.

Profile on a slow device or with CPU throttling — your development machine hides the problems your users feel on a budget phone.
lessons.task: Run Lighthouse on the Skillzify homepage and the Code Studio page, and record the three lowest-scoring opportunities on each. Then record a Performance trace while opening a lesson, find the single longest task, and write a one-paragraph fix proposal for it — with a before-and-after measurement plan, not just an opinion.
checks: What is a long task, and why does 50ms matter?
A JavaScript block over 50ms on the main thread; beyond that, taps and scrolls visibly stall because the browser cannot respond while the task runs.
What is INP in one sentence?
How quickly the page visibly responds after a user interaction — the responsiveness number users actually feel.
interview: Lighthouse says 95 but users on cheap phones complain it feels slow. What do you trust?
The users. Lighthouse runs in lab conditions; real-device traces and field INP data reflect the throttled CPUs and networks your users actually have.
What causes layout thrash, and what is the fix?
Alternating layout reads and style writes in a loop, forcing a recalculation each time. Fix: batch all reads first, then all writes.

lessons.sub: Structured concurrency: the reason your app never freezes or leaks
lessons.goal: By the end you can launch work on the right dispatcher, use async and await for parallel calls, handle cancellation correctly, and explain why viewModelScope exists.
lessons.body:
1. A coroutine is a lightweight thread you can pause

A coroutine is a computation that can suspend — pause while waiting for a network call or a database read — without blocking its thread, and resume when the result arrives. Thousands of coroutines can share a small pool of threads, which is why Android apps use them for everything asynchronous. The suspend keyword marks functions that may pause, and only another suspend function or a coroutine builder may call them — the compiler enforces the discipline, so asynchronous code cannot accidentally run on the wrong thread.

2. Dispatchers decide where work runs

Three dispatchers cover nearly everything: Main for UI updates, IO for network and disk, Default for CPU-heavy computation. withContext switches dispatcher inside a suspend function, so a Firestore fetch runs on IO and the result returns to Main for display. The classic bug is doing network work on Main — the app freezes — or updating UI from IO — which crashes. Skillzify's Android app fetches the user document on IO and updates the Compose state on Main, and that two-line pattern is most of what dispatchers are for.

3. Structured concurrency: children cannot outlive their parent

Coroutines launched in a scope are children of that scope: when the scope is cancelled, every child is cancelled too. viewModelScope lives as long as the ViewModel, so a sync job started from a screen dies automatically when the screen's ViewModel is cleared — no leaked network calls updating a dead UI. async returns a Deferred you await for parallel work — fetch the user document and the leaderboard concurrently, then combine — and cancellation propagates through await, which is why you should check for it instead of swallowing CancellationException in a generic catch.

class ProgressViewModel : ViewModel() {
  fun load(uid: String) {
    viewModelScope.launch {
      val user = async(Dispatchers.IO) { repo.getUser(uid) }
      val board = async(Dispatchers.IO) { repo.getLeaderboard() }
      val (u, b) = user.await() to board.await() // parallel, then combine
      _state.value = UiState(u, b) // back on Main automatically
    }
  }
}
// Never catch CancellationException as a generic error: rethrow it.

Flow is the coroutine answer to streams: a cold flow of values over time, collected in the UI with collectAsStateWithLifecycle, cancelled automatically when the screen leaves.
lessons.task: In the Skillzify Android app, rewrite a screen's data loading to use viewModelScope with two parallel async calls — user document and leaderboard — combined with await. Then rotate the device mid-load and confirm no crash and no duplicate request. Finally, add a 3-second timeout with withTimeout and verify cancellation cleans up.
checks: What does structured concurrency guarantee that raw threads do not?
Child coroutines are tied to their parent scope: cancelling the scope cancels all children, so work cannot outlive the screen or ViewModel that started it.
Why should you never swallow CancellationException in a generic catch?
It is how cancellation propagates. Catching it as an ordinary error breaks structured cancellation and leaves work running after its scope died.
interview: launch vs async — when is each right?
launch for fire-and-forget work with no result; async when you need the result, usually awaited alongside other parallel calls.
How do you load data in a ViewModel so rotation does not refetch?
Launch in viewModelScope, which survives configuration changes, and expose the result as StateFlow collected by the UI.

lessons.sub: State hoisting, recomposition, and lists that scroll at 60fps
lessons.goal: By the end you can hoist state correctly, use LazyColumn with stable keys, explain recomposition, and avoid the state bugs that make Compose screens behave strangely.
lessons.body:
1. State is a value plus a change notification

In Compose, state is created with remember and mutableStateOf: a value the UI reads, and a setter that triggers recomposition — the framework re-running the composables that read the value. remember keeps the value across recompositions; without it, the state resets every time the screen redraws. derivedStateOf computes a value from other state and only recomputes when its inputs change, which is how you keep expensive derivations — like a filtered lesson list — from running on every keystroke.

2. State hoisting: state lives above the composable that uses it

Hoisting means moving state up to the caller and passing the value and an on-change callback down. A LessonCard does not own whether it is done; the screen owns the list of done lessons and passes done plus onToggle down. The card becomes stateless and reusable, the screen becomes the single source of truth, and the same screen can drive the card from a ViewModel's StateFlow. When two composables need the same state, hoist it to their common ancestor — that rule resolves most Compose state confusion.

3. Lists: LazyColumn, keys, and recomposition scope

LazyColumn renders only visible items, which is why a 250-lesson list scrolls smoothly: off-screen rows do not exist yet. Give each item a stable key — the lesson ID — so Compose can track identity across reordering and filtering instead of confusing one row for another. Recomposition is smart but not magic: reading state in a small composable confines the redraw to that composable, while reading it at the top of a screen redraws everything below. Keep state reads as low in the tree as possible.

@Composable
fun LessonList(lessons: List<Lesson>, done: Set<String>, onToggle: (String) -> Unit) {
  LazyColumn {
    items(lessons, key = { it.id }) { lesson ->
      LessonRow(
        lesson = lesson,
        isDone = lesson.id in done, // state read low in the tree
        onToggle = { onToggle(lesson.id) }
      )
    }
  }
}
// State lives in the ViewModel; the list only receives values + callbacks.

The mental model in one line: the UI is a function of state, recomposition re-runs the function, and keys tell it which rows survived.
lessons.task: Build a Compose screen showing 250 lessons in a LazyColumn with stable keys, driven by a ViewModel StateFlow of completed IDs. Add a search field that filters the list through derivedStateOf. Verify three things: toggling a lesson updates only its row, filtering keeps the correct done states, and rotation preserves the search text.
checks: What is state hoisting, and why does it make a composable reusable?
Moving state to the caller and passing value plus callback down. The composable becomes stateless, so any screen can drive it with its own state.
Why does LazyColumn need a stable key per item?
So Compose tracks each row's identity across filtering and reordering; without keys it can attach the wrong state to the wrong row.
interview: What triggers recomposition, and how do you keep it cheap?
Reading a State value during composition schedules a re-run of the composables that read it. Keep reads low in the tree and use derivedStateOf for expensive derivations.
remember vs rememberSaveable — when does the difference matter?
remember survives recomposition only; rememberSaveable also survives configuration changes and process death, so it is the right choice for input text.

lessons.sub: Routes, arguments, deep links, and a back stack that behaves
lessons.goal: By the end you can define a NavHost with typed routes and arguments, handle deep links into a lesson, manage the back stack deliberately, and explain when to use nested graphs.
lessons.body:
1. Navigation is a graph of routes

Compose Navigation models an app as a graph: destinations are routes — strings like lesson/{lessonId} — and the NavHost renders the current destination while the back stack remembers where you came from. Arguments travel in the route itself, so a lesson screen receives its ID from the route and loads its data from the ViewModel. Type-safe navigation wraps those strings in serializable route classes, so a missing argument becomes a compile error instead of a runtime crash on a user's phone.

2. Deep links: the outside world enters at any screen

A deep link is a URL that opens a specific screen — a shared lesson link that opens the lesson directly instead of the home screen. You declare the URI pattern on the destination, and the system delivers the arguments the same way a manual navigation would. The discipline is making every destination work standalone: a lesson screen opened from a link must load its data from the ID alone, not depend on state set by the previous screen. That constraint improves the whole app, because every screen becomes independently loadable.

3. The back stack is a user promise

Users expect Back to undo navigation, not to exit the app unexpectedly or loop forever. Manage the stack deliberately: popUpTo when a login flow completes so Back never returns to the login screen, launchSingleTop so tapping the same bottom-nav item does not stack duplicates, and saveState so returning to a tab restores its scroll position. Nested graphs group related destinations — the whole auth flow, the whole lesson flow — so a single popUpTo can clear an entire section.

@Serializable data class LessonRoute(val lessonId: String)

NavHost(navController, startDestination = HomeRoute) {
  composable<HomeRoute> { HomeScreen(onLesson = { id ->
    navController.navigate(LessonRoute(id)) }) }
  composable<LessonRoute> { backStackEntry ->
    val route = backStackEntry.toRoute<LessonRoute>()
    LessonScreen(lessonId = route.lessonId)
  }
}
// Deep link: add a navDeepLink to LessonRoute for lesson URLs.

Test navigation the way users break it: deep link in, press Back, rotate, and confirm every path lands somewhere sensible.
lessons.task: Add type-safe navigation to the Skillzify Android app: a Home route and a LessonRoute with a lessonId argument, plus a deep link pattern so a shared lesson URL opens the lesson directly. Test the awkward paths: deep link then Back, bottom-nav re-tap, and rotation on the lesson screen.
checks: Why should a screen opened by a deep link load its data from the route argument alone?
Because no previous screen ran to set up state. The route argument is the only guaranteed input, so the screen must be independently loadable.
What do popUpTo and launchSingleTop prevent?
popUpTo clears destinations so Back never returns to a completed flow like login; launchSingleTop stops duplicate copies of the same screen stacking up.
interview: When would you use a nested navigation graph?
To group a flow — auth, onboarding, lessons — so one popUpTo clears the whole section and the graph reads as a feature, not a flat list of screens.
Type-safe routes vs string routes — what breaks with strings?
A typo or missing argument compiles fine and crashes at runtime. Typed routes make the compiler check destinations and arguments.

lessons.sub: SQLite with a compiler watching your back
lessons.goal: By the end you can define a Room entity, DAO and database, run suspend queries and Flow streams, and write a migration instead of wiping user data.
lessons.body:
1. Three pieces: entity, DAO, database

Room is a thin, compile-time-checked layer over SQLite. An entity is a data class annotated with its table name — each field a column, the primary key declared explicitly. A DAO is an interface whose methods carry SQL annotations: @Query for reads, @Insert and @Update for writes. The database class ties entities and DAOs together. The compiler verifies your SQL against the schema at build time, so a typo in a column name fails the build instead of crashing on a user's phone — Room's single biggest advantage over raw SQLite.

2. Coroutines and Flow are the API

DAO methods are suspend functions for one-shot work and Flow for streams: a query returning Flow of lessons re-emits automatically whenever the underlying table changes, so the UI stays current without manual refreshes. Writes run on a background dispatcher, and Room forbids main-thread database access by default — the crash you get for trying is the framework protecting you from freezing the UI. Skillzify's Android app can cache the user document locally in Room so the app opens instantly and syncs in the background, the offline-first pattern from Module 4 made concrete.

3. Migrations: never wipe user data

Changing the schema — adding a column, renaming a table — requires a migration: a version bump plus SQL that transforms the old data into the new shape. The fallback, destructive migration, deletes the whole database and every learner's cached progress with it. Write the migration, test it against a database created with the old version, and keep the schema export files in version control so Room can verify migrations automatically. Data loss is not a bug users forgive.

@Entity(tableName = "lessons")
data class LessonEntity(
  @PrimaryKey val id: String,
  val title: String,
  val section: String,
  val done: Boolean = false
)

@Dao
interface LessonDao {
  @Query("SELECT * FROM lessons WHERE section = :section")
  fun bySection(section: String): Flow<List<LessonEntity>>
  @Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE)
  suspend fun insertAll(lessons: List<LessonEntity>)
}

Room's rule of thumb: the database is the source of truth for what is on screen; the network is how it gets refreshed.
lessons.task: Add Room to the Skillzify Android app: a lessons table with a DAO, a repository that serves the UI from Room and refreshes from Firestore in the background. Then add a column for a bookmark flag with a proper migration, and verify existing data survives the upgrade.
checks: What does Room check at compile time that raw SQLite cannot?
Your SQL against the schema — a wrong column or table name fails the build instead of crashing at runtime.
Why is a destructive migration unacceptable for a learning app?
It deletes the database, wiping every learner's cached progress and offline data. A real migration preserves it.
interview: When would you expose Flow from a DAO instead of a suspend function?
When the UI must stay current: Flow re-emits on every table change, so the screen updates without manual refresh logic.
How does offline-first change your repository design?
The database becomes the source of truth for the UI; the network refreshes it in the background, and writes go to the database first, then sync.

lessons.sub: From a debug APK to a Play Store listing real users can install
lessons.goal: By the end you can build a signed release bundle, set up a Play Console listing, run a closed test track, and explain what the review process checks.
lessons.body:
1. Release builds are a different artefact

What you run on your phone is a debug APK: unsigned, unoptimised, and installable only by a developer. What the Play Store distributes is an App Bundle — an AAB — built in release mode with code shrinking, resource shrinking and a signing key that proves the app came from you. Lose that signing key and you can never update the app again under the same listing, so it lives in a keystore backed up in two places, never committed to git. Play App Signing holds the final key on Google's side; you hold the upload key.

2. The listing is a product page

A store listing needs an icon, screenshots on real device sizes, a short description that says what the app does in one breath, and a full description for search. Add a privacy policy URL, a content rating questionnaire, and the data safety section declaring what the app collects — for Skillzify, that means Firebase Auth identifiers and Firestore progress data. The data safety form is a legal statement, not marketing copy: get it wrong and the listing can be removed.

3. Test tracks before production

Never ship straight to production. Internal testing goes to your own team, closed testing to a list of real users, open testing to anyone who opts in — each a chance to catch crashes on devices you do not own. Google reviews every production release, usually within days, checking policy compliance and basic function. Staged rollouts then limit the blast radius: release to 10 percent, watch crash rates and reviews, and only then go to 100 percent.

// Release checklist, in order:
// 1. gradlew bundleRelease          - build the signed AAB
// 2. Version code +1, version name  - e.g. versionCode 3, "2.1.0"
// 3. Internal track                 - install it yourself, on a real phone
// 4. Closed track                   - 10+ testers, a week of real use
// 5. Production, staged rollout     - 10 percent, watch crashes, then 100 percent
// Signing key: backed up offline, never in git, never shared.

Version codes only go up, and a published version can never be unpublished into the same code — every release is a commitment.
lessons.task: Prepare the Skillzify Android app for release: bump the version code and name, build a signed release bundle, and write the full store listing — title, short and full description, and a data safety declaration for Auth and Firestore data. Upload it to the internal test track and install it from there on a real device.
checks: Why is the signing key the most important file in a release?
Without it you cannot publish updates under the same listing. Lose it and the app is effectively orphaned.
Why ship to a closed test track before production?
Real users on real devices find crashes and policy issues you cannot, and a staged rollout limits the damage if something still slips through.
interview: AAB vs APK — why does Google prefer bundles?
An AAB lets Google generate optimised APKs per device — only the needed screen densities and CPU architectures — so users download less.
Your release is rejected in review. What do you do first?
Read the rejection reason exactly, fix the policy issue — often the data safety form or a permission — and resubmit. Never resubmit unchanged hoping for a different reviewer.
